Éxilés ouïghours : la peur permanente: Uyghur Exiles: Living in Permanent Fear
« La situation là-bas est tellement crit: “The situation over there is so dire that it’s hard to believe this kind of thing is still possible in the 21st century”
Erkin Kurban, un membre de la communauté: Erkin Kurban, a member of Montréal’s Uyghur community
Les Ouïghours sont une ethnie musulmane: The Uyghurs are a Sunni Muslim ethnic group living in the Xinjiang autonomous region (also called East Turkestan), in northwestern China. Turkic-speaking, the Uyghur population, a minority in China but a majority in Xinjiang, is also present in Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Turkey. Because their people are persecuted in China, many Uyghurs have found refuge abroad, including in Canada.
C’est le cas d’Erkin Kurban, un membre d: Such is the case of Erkin Kurban, a member of Montréal’s Uyghur community, which numbers a few hundred people. Having arrived in Canada in 1999, this man in his seventies belongs to the first generation of Uyghurs to settle in the country. According to available data, there are about a thousand Uyghurs in Canada.
Le chapeau traditionnel enfoncé sur la t: His traditional hat pulled down on his head, Mr. Kurban has a lot to say.
« La situation là-bas est tellement crit: “The situation over there is so dire that it’s hard to believe this kind of thing is still possible in the 21st century,” he says, before pointing out that China treats the Uyghurs with a physical and psychological brutality that defies explanation. “I don’t even have the words to describe what’s going on over there,” he lets out, looking dejected.
À des milliers de kilomètres du Xinjiang: Thousands of kilometres from Xinjiang, the situation in this autonomous region of China keeps Canada’s Uyghurs awake at night. “We have family over there; it’s hard to be here knowing that our people are being persecuted,” says Pakyar (not his real name), who acts as interpreter for Mr. Kurban. While the “luckiest” manage to get news of the situation from their family members, most Uyghurs in Canada don’t dare ask their loved ones what is happening in Xinjiang because of the heightened surveillance carried out by Beijing.
Les raisons semblent être multiples, mai: The reasons seem to be many, but the most important are geopolitical and economic, according to Mr. Kurban. “Our region is vast and well situated geographically. It is very rich in natural resources. There is oil, natural gas, strategic minerals – in short, everything China needs to fuel its economy and strengthen its power,” he explains. Xinjiang is undeniably strategic, bordering Russia, India, Mongolia, Kazakhstan, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan.
Depuis plusieurs années, la Chine a entr: For several years, China has been working to make up for its development lag by turning this territory into the bridgehead of its trade with Central Asia. Many foreign and Chinese multinationals have set up there. In Mr. Kurban’s view, this explains Beijing’s behaviour toward the Uyghurs, who are demanding their autonomy.
« La Chine ne peut et ne veut pas nous l: “China cannot and will not let us determine our own destiny,” he says. “We have become an obstacle to its economic growth.” Many experts share this view, especially since Xinjiang occupies a central place in the monumental “New Silk Road” project launched by Chinese President Xi Jinping. A student at McGill University, Zapaer Alip coordinates Uyghur International Support (Soutien international aux Ouïghours), a cultural association that has turned into an organization defending Uyghur rights. According to him, many Uyghur families in Canada have practically stopped communicating with relatives who stayed in Xinjiang.
« Toutes les communications sont surveil: “All communications are monitored, and people over there avoid saying things that could put them in a difficult situation,” he explains. That is also his own case, he admitted to us over coffee. Zapaer is glad to see that the international and Canadian press are talking more and more often about the situation of the Uyghurs. “Before, Canadians had a vague idea of what was happening; they didn’t grasp the scale of it,” he says. “Thanks to the detailed reports produced by international NGOs and the New York Times, among others, Canadians now understand.”
Selon lui, cela constitue un signe d’esp: In his view, this is a sign of hope, even if China has no intention of giving in anytime soon to international pressure, which is becoming more and more insistent. For Mr. Kurban, “the fight must go on.” He says he is proud to see his children getting involved in the cause. And on the pressure the Chinese government puts on Uyghurs in Canada who denounce the situation in Xinjiang, he says: “I have suffered so much that I have forgotten how to be afraid.” In an irony of history, Erkin, his first name, means “free” in the Uyghur language…
Dans le Xinjiang, les visées indépendant: In Xinjiang, the Uyghurs’ aspirations for independence have for decades run up against the Chinese government’s repressive policies. In its report Eradicating Ideological Viruses: China’s Campaign of Repression Against Xinjiang’s Muslims, the American NGO Human Rights Watch (HRW) concludes that the Chinese government is failing to respect the Uyghurs’ most basic rights. “Throughout the region, the 13 million members of the Turkic Muslim population are subjected to forced political indoctrination, collective punishment, religious restrictions and mass surveillance, in violation of international human rights law,” the report states.
De son côté, la Chine justifie sa politi: For its part, China justifies its policy as a fight against Islamic terrorism and a concern to deradicalize the Uyghurs. Canada’s former ambassador to China, Guy Saint-Jacques, believes this argument is not without merit. “There were several attacks in China carried out by Uyghurs, and you can understand the measures that were taken to stop those acts,” he says. While Mr. Saint-Jacques understands the approach Beijing took a few years ago, he refuses to endorse the policy the Chinese government is currently pursuing toward the Uyghurs.
« Ce qui se passe là-bas n’a pas de sens: “What is happening there makes no sense and cannot be justified by a concern to fight terrorism,” he says. Because, in addition to arbitrary detention, torture and mistreatment, there are reports of forced sterilization of women, apparently in order to reduce the Uyghur population.
Kurban et Alip attendent beaucoup du gou: Kurban and Alip expect a lot from the Government of Canada. They agree that Ottawa must act to put an end to the marginalization of the Uyghurs in China. Uyghur International Support has proposed a 12-point political and humanitarian plan “to support marginalized Uyghur populations.” “Canada must send a clear and firm message to China on this,” says Mr. Kurban, who nevertheless seems to have few illusions about it. In his view, “China does not respect Canada.” He points to something he experienced himself. “When I went to China in 2006, I was summoned by the security services. When I showed them my Canadian passport, they threw it on the ground and told me they didn’t give a damn. As if to tell me that Canada is worth nothing.” Pakyar, our interpreter, believes for his part that Canada must do something because, he argues, several minority groups are marginalized in China. “Over there, all minorities are persecuted, whether they’re Uyghur, Christian, Jewish, and so on. That’s why Canada and the other democratic countries must be urged to act. Staying silent sends the wrong signal to the Chinese government.”
Dans une lettre adressée au premier mini: In a letter addressed to Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, 68 MPs and senators asked Ottawa to impose sanctions on China. Contacted about this, Global Affairs Canada merely told La Converse that Canada has “publicly and consistently called on the Chinese government to end the repression in Xinjiang.”
Du côté des États-Unis, la Chambre des r: In the United States, the House of Representatives recently passed a bill calling for sanctions against China in response to the internment of Uyghurs. Does Canada have the means to impose sanctions on China? For Mr. Saint-Jacques, that is easier said than done. “Canada has not been harshly critical of China,” he observes. “The problem is that every country knows that if they are very harsh in their criticism of China, they will face economic retaliation.”
D’après lui, « la Chine est consciente q: In his view, “China is aware that most major countries need it so much for trade that no one dares take measures or impose sanctions that are too severe against it.”
Pour MM. Kurban et Alip, cela n’empêche: For Mr. Kurban and Mr. Alip, this doesn’t prevent Ottawa from making it clear to Beijing that it should change its behaviour toward the Uyghurs. Mr. Saint-Jacques, for his part, believes Canada should adopt a multilateral approach: “Canada should work with other allied countries to develop a common position on China, especially in light of what we now know about what is happening in Xinjiang.” Liberal MP Sameer Zuberi, who sat on the Subcommittee on International Human Rights of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and International Development, shares that view.
M. Zuberi, qui se dit très préoccupé par: Mr. Zuberi, who says he is deeply concerned about the situation of the Uyghurs – which he calls “unbearable” – believes Canada is not powerful enough to stand up to China alone. “We must join forces with other powers to bring China to its senses […] What the Chinese government is doing must stop,” he says.
<strong>La solidarité silencieuse des au: The silent solidarity of other Chinese people
Les Ouïghours de Montréal ne sont pas se: Montréal’s Uyghurs are not alone in their fight. According to Mr. Alip and Pakyar, many Chinese people support their cause, especially among the younger generation. “What do you think of the situation of the Uyghurs in Xinjiang?” we asked about ten members of the Chinese diaspora in Montréal’s Chinatown. Most preferred not to answer; only two people subtly let us understand that they did not endorse it.
Une solidarité silencieuse pour ne pas s: It is a silent solidarity, so as not to draw the wrath of Beijing, which monitors not only what happens inside its borders, but also what happens beyond them. This is the case for Min (not her real name), a 26-year-old Chinese woman studying at McGill University. She admitted in a whisper that she supports the Uyghur cause.
« Je les soutiens moralement, mais j’ai: “I support them morally, but I’m afraid to speak out on social media,” she confided to us during an interview she refused to let us record, for fear of leaving traces of her testimony. “I have to be careful; my grandparents are still in China. My grandfather fought against Japan during the war. I don’t want them to be harmed.
Je sais que, si je parle publiquement, o: I know that if I speak publicly, it would be easy to track me down.” Like most Chinese people in the diaspora, Min is aware of the consequences her stand could have in a China where those in power are allergic to any criticism.
« Mon gouvernement a tellement de police: “My government has so much online police and so much information on people,” the student explains. “It wouldn’t be hard for them to find me and go after my family. My parents live in Vancouver. We communicate on WeChat, and I’m afraid to talk about it with them. I know the Chinese government monitors conversations. We never speak negatively about China when we communicate online.”
Au moment d’écrire ces lignes, le consul: At the time of writing, the Consulate General of China in Montréal had still not responded to our interview requests.
